title: Buzzer melody
desc: Piezo buzzer plays tunes like Ode to Joy
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno (or compatible board) — Nerokas (nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Passive piezo buzzer (must be passive, not active — passive buzzers can play different pitches) — Pixel Electronics (pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Half-size or full-size breadboard — Nerokas (nerokas.co.ke)
  • 2 x Male-to-male jumper wires — Nerokas (nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB cable (A-to-B for Uno, or appropriate cable for your board) — Pixel Electronics (pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x 100 ohm resistor (optional, protects the buzzer and softens volume) — Nerokas (nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Laptop or computer with Arduino IDE installed

How It Works

Sound is just air vibrating very quickly. A piezo buzzer has a tiny disc inside that can flex back and forth when electricity is applied to it. If the disc flexes slowly, we hear a low note. If it flexes quickly, we hear a high note. The number of times it flexes per second is called frequency, measured in Hertz (Hz). For example, the musical note "A" that orchestras tune to vibrates 440 times every second — that's 440 Hz.

The Arduino cannot "play music" on its own — it can only turn a pin ON and OFF very fast. The built-in tone() function does this for us: we tell it which pin the buzzer is on and which frequency we want, and Arduino rapidly switches that pin on and off at exactly that frequency, making the buzzer disc vibrate at that speed. To play a tune, we store a list (an array) of note frequencies and a matching list of how long each note should last, then use a loop to step through the list, calling tone() for each note in turn and pausing briefly before moving to the next one.

This project introduces three ideas that appear in almost every Arduino project afterwards: using a built-in function (tone()), storing multiple related values in an array, and using a for loop to process a list of data one item at a time.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Lay out all materials on the table and check that the buzzer is a passive buzzer (it should have no visible sticker/dome marking it as "active" — active buzzers can only make one beeping sound and cannot play a melody).
  2. Insert the buzzer into the breadboard so its two legs sit in two different rows.
  3. Identify the buzzer's positive leg (often marked with a "+" or slightly longer leg) and connect it with a jumper wire to Arduino digital pin 8.
  4. Connect the buzzer's negative leg to the Arduino's GND pin using the second jumper wire. If using the optional resistor, place it in series between the buzzer and pin 8.
  5. Double-check the wiring before connecting power — loose wires are the most common cause of "no sound".
  6. Connect the Arduino to the computer with the USB cable.
  7. Open the Arduino IDE, select the correct board and port under the Tools menu.
  8. Create a new sketch and paste in the full code provided below.
  9. Click Upload and wait for "Done uploading" to appear at the bottom of the IDE.
  10. Listen carefully — the buzzer should play the opening phrase of "Ode to Joy". Ask students to hum along or tap the rhythm with their finger.
  11. Pause the demonstration and open the code together. Point out the two arrays (melody[] and noteDurations[]) and explain that each position in one array matches the same position in the other.
  12. Have students change a few numbers in the melody[] array and re-upload to hear how the tune changes — this makes the link between code and sound concrete.

Full Code

// Buzzer Melody: Ode to Joy
// Uses the built-in tone() function to play a sequence of musical notes

// Musical note frequencies in Hertz (Hz).
// These numbers tell the buzzer how fast to vibrate for each note.
#define NOTE_C4  262
#define NOTE_D4  294
#define NOTE_E4  330
#define NOTE_F4  349
#define NOTE_G4  392

const int buzzerPin = 8; // digital pin connected to the buzzer's positive leg

// List of notes to play, in order (this is an "array")
int melody[] = {
  NOTE_E4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_F4, NOTE_G4,
  NOTE_G4, NOTE_F4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_D4,
  NOTE_C4, NOTE_C4, NOTE_D4, NOTE_E4,
  NOTE_E4, NOTE_D4, NOTE_D4,
  NOTE_E4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_F4, NOTE_G4,
  NOTE_G4, NOTE_F4, NOTE_E4, NOTE_D4,
  NOTE_C4, NOTE_C4, NOTE_D4, NOTE_E4,
  NOTE_D4, NOTE_C4, NOTE_C4
};

// How long each note lasts. 4 = quarter note, 2 = half note (twice as long).
// This array must have the SAME NUMBER of items as melody[], in the same order.
int noteDurations[] = {
  4, 4, 4, 4,
  4, 4, 4, 4,
  4, 4, 4, 4,
  4, 4, 2,
  4, 4, 4, 4,
  4, 4, 4, 4,
  4, 4, 4, 4,
  4, 4, 2
};

// Work out how many notes are in the melody automatically,
// so we don't have to count them by hand and risk a mistake.
const int totalNotes = sizeof(melody) / sizeof(melody[0]);

void setup() {
  // No pinMode() is required for tone() -- it manages the pin automatically.
  // We keep setup() empty here on purpose; the tune plays in loop().
}

void loop() {
  // Step through every note in the melody, one at a time
  for (int thisNote = 0; thisNote < totalNotes; thisNote++) {

    // Convert the "4 = quarter note" style duration into milliseconds.
    // 1000 ms / 4 = 250 ms for a quarter note, 1000 / 2 = 500 ms for a half note.
    int noteDuration = 1000 / noteDurations[thisNote];

    // Play this note on the buzzer pin for noteDuration milliseconds
    tone(buzzerPin, melody[thisNote], noteDuration);

    // Leave a short gap between notes so they don't blur into each other.
    // 1.30 gives a small natural pause after each note.
    int pauseBetweenNotes = noteDuration * 1.30;
    delay(pauseBetweenNotes);

    // Stop the tone before moving to the next note
    noTone(buzzerPin);
  }

  delay(2000); // wait 2 seconds before repeating the whole tune
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
No sound at allBuzzer legs swapped, loose jumper wire, or wrong pin number in codeCheck that pin 8 in the code matches the actual wired pin, and reseat both jumper wires firmly
Buzzer only makes one clicking/beeping sound, tune doesn't play properlyAn active buzzer is being used instead of a passive oneSwap in a passive piezo buzzer — active buzzers cannot change pitch
Melody sounds wrong, notes seem jumbled or cut off oddlymelody[] and noteDurations[] arrays don't have the same number of entriesCount both arrays carefully and make sure every note has a matching duration in the same position
Code won't compile / red error messageMissing comma, missing semicolon, or extra bracket in the arraysCompare the arrays character-by-character with the sample code and fix punctuation
Sound is very quiet or distortedNo series resistor, or buzzer resting loosely in the breadboardPush the buzzer legs firmly into the breadboard; add the 100 ohm resistor if available
Tune plays once then Arduino seems to freeze/stopStudents assume it should loop instantly but forget the 2 second pause is intentionalExplain that delay(2000) at the end of loop() is a deliberate pause before repeating
